name: Shave your head

lead: Shaving your head removes the patchy, thinning or receding hair and leaves an even scalp or short uniform length. The payoff is a clean, deliberate look in place of a partial one, and proponents say it reads as confident.

It works by changing how the remaining hair and scalp appear, not by changing hair growth. Studies of how bald or shaved men are perceived have reached different results across studies and cultures, and no clinical trials of head shaving as an appearance strategy were found.

paras: People use clippers at a short uniform length or a razor for a smooth scalp, often as an alternative to concealing or treating hair loss. The result is visible immediately and is kept up by repeating the shave as hair grows back. Many pair it with beard grooming and sun protection for the scalp.

Documented risks are minor: razor irritation or nicks, and sun exposure on a newly uncovered scalp, where dermatology bodies commonly advise sun protection. It does not treat hair loss, which continues underneath.

angle.text: Men with thinning or receding hair shave or clip their heads to replace a patchy look with a clean, even one. Proponents say it reads as confident. The change is visible straight away, and perception research on bald men gives mixed results.

lead: Shaving the head is a style approach, discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a response to hair loss, in which a person with thinning or receding hair removes the remaining hair to a uniform short length or to the skin rather than trying to conceal or treat the loss. Proponents describe it as a way to present a deliberate, clean look instead of a partial one.[1]

Head shaving has a long history across cultures, with records from ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and it carries varied meanings including religious practice, military uniformity, punishment, sport, solidarity with cancer patients and fashion.[1] For men with pattern hair loss, encyclopedic sources list shaving the head as one way to improve the appearance of the condition, and note a proposed social theory that fully bald men may be read as signaling dominance or high status; survey results on how bald men are rated have differed between studies and cultures.[2]
No clinical studies specifically testing head shaving as an appearance strategy were identified for this article, and sources on the topic are limited.

paras: The practice ranges from clipping hair to a very short uniform length to shaving the scalp smooth with a razor or foil shaver. In appearance discussions it is often paired with the idea of embracing baldness, as opposed to treatments, hairpieces or comb-over styles.[2]

Records of head shaving date to ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome. Egyptian priests removed body hair, and Romans offered a first shave to the gods.[1] Many Buddhist, Hindu and Hare Krishna practitioners shave their heads, often on entering a religious order.[1]

In ancient Greece and much of Babylon, a shaved head marked enslaved people, and in later periods shaving has been used as a punishment or humiliation, including in prisons and in post-war France.[1] Militaries commonly shave recruits' heads, citing hygiene and uniformity.[1]

Yul Brynner is credited with popularising the look in the 1950s, and shaved heads have been adopted by several subcultures.[1] People also shave their heads in solidarity with cancer patients and to raise funds.[1] Shaving by people with hair loss conditions such as alopecia areata has become more socially accepted since the 1990s.[1]

Male pattern hair loss is described as a moderately stressful condition that can reduce body-image satisfaction, although most men are reported to cope.[2] One proposed social theory holds that men who shave to complete baldness signal dominance, high status or longevity.[2]

Studies on how others perceive bald men conflict: a 2001 South Korean study found most people rated balding men as less attractive, while a 2002 survey of Welsh women rated bald and gray-haired men as quite desirable.[2] Encyclopedia authors note that many of these sources are primary studies rather than reviews.[2]

Within appearance communities, shaving is commonly framed as the alternative to treatment for those who prefer not to use or continue medications, and as a style option when hair loss is advanced. Reports of how it is received vary by individual head shape, skin and facial features, and no controlled studies were found on these claims.
No studies found. Related published work concerns how observers rate balding men generally, with conflicting results across cultures.[2]

lore.intro: The practice is discussed in hair-loss and style threads as a response to progressive thinning, though no community threads are cited here.
